claim: The meta-analysis included 65 field studies across the Earth's major forest ecosystems.
source: With a meta-analysis including 65 field studies across the Earth's major forest ecosystems, we show here that decomposition was faster when litter was composed of more than one species.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of studies included in the meta-analysis.

claim: Decomposition was faster when litter was composed of more than one species.
source: With a meta-analysis including 65 field studies across the Earth's major forest ecosystems, we show here that decomposition was faster when litter was composed of more than one species.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the meta-analysis data.

claim: Positive biodiversity effects on decomposition were mostly driven by temperate forests.
source: These positive biodiversity effects were mostly driven by temperate forests but were more variable in other forests.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Litter mixture effects emerged most strongly in early decomposition stages.
source: Litter mixture effects emerged most strongly in early decomposition stages and were related to divergence in litter quality.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Litter mixture effects were related to divergence in litter quality.
source: Litter mixture effects emerged most strongly in early decomposition stages and were related to divergence in litter quality.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Litter diversity accelerated nitrogen release.
source: Litter diversity also accelerated nitrogen, but not phosphorus release, potentially indicating a decoupling of nitrogen and phosphorus cycling and perhaps a shift in ecosystem nutrient limitation with changing biodiversity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Litter diversity did not accelerate phosphorus release.
source: Litter diversity also accelerated nitrogen, but not phosphorus release, potentially indicating a decoupling of nitrogen and phosphorus cycling and perhaps a shift in ecosystem nutrient limitation with changing biodiversity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The differential effects on nitrogen and phosphorus release potentially indicate a decoupling of nitrogen and phosphorus cycling.
source: Litter diversity also accelerated nitrogen, but not phosphorus release, potentially indicating a decoupling of nitrogen and phosphorus cycling and perhaps a shift in ecosystem nutrient limitation with changing biodiversity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data patterns.

claim: The differential effects on nitrogen and phosphorus release may indicate a shift in ecosystem nutrient limitation with changing biodiversity.
source: Litter diversity also accelerated nitrogen, but not phosphorus release, potentially indicating a decoupling of nitrogen and phosphorus cycling and perhaps a shift in ecosystem nutrient limitation with changing biodiversity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data patterns.

claim: Forests mediate biosphere-atmosphere carbon dynamics via primary productivity.
source: Forests mediate biosphere-atmosphere carbon (C) dynamics via primary productivity (Huang et al., 2018; Liang et al., 2016) and decomposition (Handa et al., 2014; Hooper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Forests mediate biosphere-atmosphere carbon dynamics via decomposition.
source: Forests mediate biosphere-atmosphere carbon (C) dynamics via primary productivity (Huang et al., 2018; Liang et al., 2016) and decomposition (Handa et al., 2014; Hooper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Litter mixtures can decompose at different rates than would be predicted from the rates of the individual component species.
source: Litter mixtures can decompose at different rates than would be predicted from the rates of the individual component species, resulting in non-additive effects with either faster (synergistic effects) or slower (antagonistic effects) decomposition (Gartner and Cardon, 2004; Wardle et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Synergistic effects may result from fungi-driven nitrogen transfer among different litter types.
source: Synergistic effects may result from fungi-driven nitrogen (N) transfer among different litter types (Lummer et al., 2012; Schimel and Hättenschwiler, 2007) or through complementary resource use among microbial decomposers or detritivores (Gessner et al., 2010; Vos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Synergistic effects may result from complementary resource use among microbial decomposers or detritivores.
source: Synergistic effects may result from fungi-driven nitrogen (N) transfer among different litter types (Lummer et al., 2012; Schimel and Hättenschwiler, 2007) or through complementary resource use among microbial decomposers or detritivores (Gessner et al., 2010; Vos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Antagonistic effects may result from inhibiting or recalcitrant compounds present in one litter type that negatively affect the decomposition of the whole mixture of litter.
source: On the other hand, antagonistic effects may result from inhibiting or recalcitrant compounds (e.g. lignin and polyphenols) present in one litter type that negatively affect the decomposition of the whole mixture of litter (Hättenschwiler et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The dataset encompassed 284 plant species combinations from 65 field studies on decomposition of leaf litter mixtures in five forest biomes.
source: Towards this goal, we assembled a global dataset encompassing 284 plant species combinations from 65 field studies on decomposition of leaf litter mixtures in five forest biomes (Figure 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The average mass loss measured at final harvest was higher in litter mixtures compared to those expected from single species litter.
source: Across biomes, the average mass loss and N release measured at final harvest (i.e. excluding data from intermediate harvests in the studies with several harvest dates) were higher in litter mixtures compared to those expected from single species litter, but there was no effect on P release (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the meta-analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The average nitrogen release measured at final harvest was higher in litter mixtures compared to those expected from single species litter.
source: Across biomes, the average mass loss and N release measured at final harvest (i.e. excluding data from intermediate harvests in the studies with several harvest dates) were higher in litter mixtures compared to those expected from single species litter, but there was no effect on P release (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the meta-analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There was no effect of litter mixtures on phosphorus release at final harvest.
source: Across biomes, the average mass loss and N release measured at final harvest (i.e. excluding data from intermediate harvests in the studies with several harvest dates) were higher in litter mixtures compared to those expected from single species litter, but there was no effect on P release (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the meta-analysis data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The effect size for mass loss was significantly positive in temperate forests.
source: Except for boreal forests, the effect size for mass loss was generally positive but was only significantly so in temperate and subtropical forests.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The effect size for mass loss was significantly positive in subtropical forests.
source: Except for boreal forests, the effect size for mass loss was generally positive but was only significantly so in temperate and subtropical forests.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The effect size for nitrogen release was significantly positive for temperate forests.
source: The effect size for N release was significantly positive for temperate forests, showed a positive trend for boreal forests and a negative trend for subtropical forests (there was only one observation in each of tropical and Mediterranean forests).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The effect size for nitrogen release showed a positive trend for boreal forests.
source: The effect size for N release was significantly positive for temperate forests, showed a positive trend for boreal forests and a negative trend for subtropical forests (there was only one observation in each of tropical and Mediterranean forests).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The effect size for nitrogen release showed a negative trend for subtropical forests.
source: The effect size for N release was significantly positive for temperate forests, showed a positive trend for boreal forests and a negative trend for subtropical forests (there was only one observation in each of tropical and Mediterranean forests).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Synergistic effects on mass loss were particularly clear in the range from 10% to 40% of mass loss with effect sizes of 7% to 10%.
source: Regarding 10% mass loss intervals, the synergistic effects on mass loss were particularly clear in the range from 10% to 40% of mass loss (effect sizes: 7% to 10%), and decreased sharply in the range from 40% to 60% of mass loss (effect sizes: 2% to 3%) and further decreased gradually in later decomposition stages beyond 60% mass loss (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Synergistic effects on mass loss decreased sharply in the range from 40% to 60% of mass loss with effect sizes of 2% to 3%.
source: Regarding 10% mass loss intervals, the synergistic effects on mass loss were particularly clear in the range from 10% to 40% of mass loss (effect sizes: 7% to 10%), and decreased sharply in the range from 40% to 60% of mass loss (effect sizes: 2% to 3%) and further decreased gradually in later decomposition stages beyond 60% mass loss (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: At mass losses below 10% and above 60%, litter mixing had purely additive effects on mass loss.
source: At mass losses below 10% and above 60%, litter mixing had purely additive effects on mass loss.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Antagonistic effects on nitrogen release were found at 0–10% mass loss.
source: We found antagonistic effects on N release at 0–10% mass loss, additive effects during the three intervals from 10–20%, 40–50% and 60–70% mass loss, and synergistic effects during the four intervals from 20–30%, 30–40%, 50–60% and 70–100% (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Additive effects on nitrogen release were found during the intervals from 10–20%, 40–50% and 60–70% mass loss.
source: We found antagonistic effects on N release at 0–10% mass loss, additive effects during the three intervals from 10–20%, 40–50% and 60–70% mass loss, and synergistic effects during the four intervals from 20–30%, 30–40%, 50–60% and 70–100% (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Synergistic effects on nitrogen release were found during the intervals from 20–30%, 30–40%, 50–60% and 70–100% mass loss.
source: We found antagonistic effects on N release at 0–10% mass loss, additive effects during the three intervals from 10–20%, 40–50% and 60–70% mass loss, and synergistic effects during the four intervals from 20–30%, 30–40%, 50–60% and 70–100% (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Litter mixing effects on phosphorus release were consistently additive throughout the process of decomposition.
source: The litter mixing effects on P release were consistently additive throughout the process of decomposition (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Nitrogen release rates from mixtures (35.4% on average) were about twice as high compared to those from single species litter (18.7% on average).
source: Relative to the initial amount of N contained in litter, N release rates from mixtures (35.4% on average) were about twice as high compared to those from single species litter (18.7% on average, p=0.042; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Phosphorus release rates from mixtures (33.2% on average) were not significantly different compared to those from single species litter (29.7% on average).
source: In contrast, P release rates from mixtures (33.2% on average) were not significantly different compared to those from single species litter (29.7% on average; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The absolute release rate of nitrogen was higher in litter mixtures compared to single species litter (4.35 mg g−1 vs. 2.51 mg g−1).
source: The absolute release rate of N was higher in litter mixtures compared to single species litter (4.35 mg g−1 vs. 2.51 mg g−1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while that of P was about the same in litter mixtures and single species litter (0.16 mg g−1 vs. 0.13 mg g−1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The absolute release rate of phosphorus was about the same in litter mixtures and single species litter (0.16 mg g−1 vs. 0.13 mg g−1).
source: The absolute release rate of N was higher in litter mixtures compared to single species litter (4.35 mg g−1 vs. 2.51 mg g−1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), while that of P was about the same in litter mixtures and single species litter (0.16 mg g−1 vs. 0.13 mg g−1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Synergistic effects emerged when litter mixtures were composed of two or three species.
source: Specifically, synergistic effects emerged when litter mixtures were composed of two (n = 196) or three (n = 41) species while additive effects predominated when four (n = 34) or six species (n = 13) were included in a mixture.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Additive effects predominated when four or six species were included in a mixture.
source: Specifically, synergistic effects emerged when litter mixtures were composed of two (n = 196) or three (n = 41) species while additive effects predominated when four (n = 34) or six species (n = 13) were included in a mixture.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Synergistic effects were present regardless of the ratio of component litter species in a mixture.
source: The synergistic effects were present regardless of the ratio (mass-based) of component litter species in a mixture, i.e. equal (n = 225) or non-equal ratios (n = 59).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Synergistic effects were found when litters from deciduous species were in the mixtures, irrespective of whether or not they were combined with evergreen species.
source: Moreover, synergistic effects were always found when litters from deciduous species were in the mixtures, irrespective of whether or not they were combined with evergreen species.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: When only evergreen species were mixed together, the effects remained additive.
source: On the contrary, when only evergreen species were mixed together, the effects remained additive.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: In natural forests, synergistic effects emerged for litter mixtures composed of the canopy tree species but not for other combinations when understory species were also included.
source: In natural forests, the synergistic effects emerged for litter mixtures composed of the canopy tree species but not for other combinations of litter mixtures when understory species were also included.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: In planted forests, the opposite pattern was found compared to natural forests regarding understory species effects.
source: However, we found the opposite pattern in planted forests (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: For mesh sizes between 1 mm and 2 mm, there was a clear synergistic effect.
source: For mesh sizes between 1 mm and 2 mm, there was a clear synergistic effect (n = 148), while smaller mesh sizes (<1 mm, n = 72) and larger mesh sizes (>2 mm, n = 109) resulted in additive effects (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Smaller mesh sizes (<1 mm) and larger mesh sizes (>2 mm) resulted in additive effects.
source: For mesh sizes between 1 mm and 2 mm, there was a clear synergistic effect (n = 148), while smaller mesh sizes (<1 mm, n = 72) and larger mesh sizes (>2 mm, n = 109) resulted in additive effects (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The effect sizes for mass loss were negatively correlated with MAP (r2 = 0.049, p<0.001).
source: The effect sizes for mass loss were negatively correlated with MAP (r2 = 0.049, p<0.001; Figure 6B), but they showed no correlation with MAT (p>0.05; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: The effect sizes for mass loss showed no correlation with MAT.
source: The effect sizes for mass loss were negatively correlated with MAP (r2 = 0.049, p<0.001; Figure 6B), but they showed no correlation with MAT (p>0.05; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: During the period of decomposition with the strongest non-additive mixing effects (10–40% mass loss), the effect sizes for mass loss were negatively correlated with the divergence in the initial N:P ratio of the litter species included in the mixtures (r2 = 0.076, p<0.05).
source: During the period of decomposition with the strongest non-additive mixing effects (10–40% mass loss), the effect sizes for mass loss were negatively correlated with the divergence in the initial N:P ratio of the litter species included in the mixtures (r2 = 0.076, p<0.05; Figure 7I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7I.

claim: There were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial P (r2 = 0.246, p<0.001).
source: In contrast, there were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial P (r2 = 0.246, p<0.001; Figure 7B), K (r2 = 0.445, p<0.001; Figure 7C), Ca (r2 = 0.360, p<0.001; Figure 7D), Mg (r2 = 0.346, p<0.001; Figure 7E), cellulose (r2 = 0.388, p<0.001; Figure 7G), and lignin:N ratio (r2 = 0.335, p<0.001; Figure 7J) among litter species present in the mixtures.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7B.

claim: There were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial K (r2 = 0.445, p<0.001).
source: In contrast, there were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial P (r2 = 0.246, p<0.001; Figure 7B), K (r2 = 0.445, p<0.001; Figure 7C), Ca (r2 = 0.360, p<0.001; Figure 7D), Mg (r2 = 0.346, p<0.001; Figure 7E), cellulose (r2 = 0.388, p<0.001; Figure 7G), and lignin:N ratio (r2 = 0.335, p<0.001; Figure 7J) among litter species present in the mixtures.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7C.

claim: There were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial Ca (r2 = 0.360, p<0.001).
source: In contrast, there were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial P (r2 = 0.246, p<0.001; Figure 7B), K (r2 = 0.445, p<0.001; Figure 7C), Ca (r2 = 0.360, p<0.001; Figure 7D), Mg (r2 = 0.346, p<0.001; Figure 7E), cellulose (r2 = 0.388, p<0.001; Figure 7G), and lignin:N ratio (r2 = 0.335, p<0.001; Figure 7J) among litter species present in the mixtures.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7D.

claim: There were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial Mg (r2 = 0.346, p<0.001).
source: In contrast, there were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial P (r2 = 0.246, p<0.001; Figure 7B), K (r2 = 0.445, p<0.001; Figure 7C), Ca (r2 = 0.360, p<0.001; Figure 7D), Mg (r2 = 0.346, p<0.001; Figure 7E), cellulose (r2 = 0.388, p<0.001; Figure 7G), and lignin:N ratio (r2 = 0.335, p<0.001; Figure 7J) among litter species present in the mixtures.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7E.

claim: There were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial cellulose (r2 = 0.388, p<0.001).
source: In contrast, there were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial P (r2 = 0.246, p<0.001; Figure 7B), K (r2 = 0.445, p<0.001; Figure 7C), Ca (r2 = 0.360, p<0.001; Figure 7D), Mg (r2 = 0.346, p<0.001; Figure 7E), cellulose (r2 = 0.388, p<0.001; Figure 7G), and lignin:N ratio (r2 = 0.335, p<0.001; Figure 7J) among litter species present in the mixtures.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7G.

claim: There were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial lignin:N ratio (r2 = 0.335, p<0.001).
source: In contrast, there were positive correlations between the effect size of litter mass loss and the divergence in initial P (r2 = 0.246, p<0.001; Figure 7B), K (r2 = 0.445, p<0.001; Figure 7C), Ca (r2 = 0.360, p<0.001; Figure 7D), Mg (r2 = 0.346, p<0.001; Figure 7E), cellulose (r2 = 0.388, p<0.001; Figure 7G), and lignin:N ratio (r2 = 0.335, p<0.001; Figure 7J) among litter species present in the mixtures.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7J.

claim: The predominant synergistic litter mixture effects for both mass loss and N release are in line with a relatively tight coupling of C and N dynamics in terrestrial ecosystems.
source: The predominant synergistic litter mixture effects for both mass loss and N release are in line with a relatively tight coupling of C and N dynamics in terrestrial ecosystems through processes such as biomass production, decomposition, and organic matter storage in soils that all operate within relatively small stoichiometric ranges (Gruber and Galloway, 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data patterns supported by citation.

claim: High amounts of rainfall may increase leaching of labile C and nutrients from decomposing litters.
source: Perhaps, high amounts of rainfall increase leaching of labile C and nutrients from decomposing litters (Pérez-Suárez et al., 2012), which would restrict non-additive interactions based on transfer and/or complementary use of nutrients and C compounds.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation.

claim: Phosphorus is less bound to complex C structures and typically released at higher rates than N during litter breakdown.
source: Phosphorus is less bound to complex C structures and typically released at higher rates than N during litter breakdown (Manzoni et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: An average of 30% of P was released from single species litters compared to 19% of N during the same period of time.
source: In our dataset, an average of 30% of P was released from single species litters compared to 19% of N during the same period of time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) confirming a more rapid P than N release.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The greater N but not P release from litter to soil pools from litter mixtures may indicate a shift in the relative availabilities of these key nutrients with a potential decoupling of N and P cycling with reduced biodiversity.
source: The greater N but not P release from litter to soil pools from litter mixtures may indicate a shift in the relative availabilities of these key nutrients with a potential decoupling of N and P cycling with reduced biodiversity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data patterns.

claim: Synergistic mixture effects may be particularly important relatively early during the decomposition process, but only after the first few months during which leaching losses usually dominate litter mass loss.
source: Synergistic mixture effects, thus, may be particularly important relatively early during the decomposition process, but only after the first few months (10% of mass loss corresponds to 2–6 months globally) during which leaching losses usually dominate litter mass loss.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data patterns.

claim: Leaching is mostly a physical process, so biological interactions driving potential mixing effects may have a limited effect during the very early stage of decomposition.
source: As leaching is mostly a physical process, biological interactions driving potential mixing effects may have a limited effect during this very early stage of decomposition.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about leaching processes.

claim: The synergistic effects decreased gradually over the decomposition process, which can be expected with converging litter quality among litter species during decomposition.
source: The synergistic effects decreased gradually over the decomposition process, which can be expected with converging litter quality among litter species during decomposition (Moore et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data patterns supported by citation.

claim: There is a clear lack of long-term mixed litter decomposition studies.
source: Moreover, there is a clear lack of long-term mixed litter decomposition studies.
evidence: This is an observation about the available literature.

claim: Only three studies measured decomposition to a mass loss of over 80% included in the meta-analysis.
source: Only three studies measured decomposition to a mass loss of over 80% included in our meta-analysis, which is too few to conclude unambiguously that there are no litter mixture effects in lignin-dominated stages of decomposition.
evidence: This is a statement about the dataset composition.

claim: Interactions could switch to antagonistic mixture effects during the lignin-dominated phase of decomposition.
source: In fact, interactions could even switch to antagonistic mixture effects during the lignin-dominated phase of decomposition (Preston et al., 2009), but further studies are required to confirm this.
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation.

claim: Distinct resource requirements of microbial decomposers and the resulting successional changes in microbial community structure and composition during decomposition may explain the temporal changes in litter mixture effects.
source: Distinct resource requirements of microbial decomposers (Allison et al., 2013; German et al., 2011) and the resulting successional changes in microbial community structure and composition during decomposition may also explain the temporal changes in litter mixture effects (Gessner et al., 2010; Wickings et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Nitrogen is often immobilized during the initial stages of decomposition, resulting in a net increase of N.
source: Nitrogen is often immobilized during the initial stages of decomposition, resulting in a net increase of N.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about nitrogen dynamics during decomposition.

claim: The dynamics of N immobilization and release may have contributed to the shifting mixing effects through time.
source: The dynamics of N immobilization and release may have contributed to the shifting mixing effects through time, which was also observed in previous studies (García-Palacios et al., 2017; Schuster and Dukes, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Nitrogen is an important driver of the synergistic effect of mixed litter decomposition via N transfer among different litter types.
source: Nitrogen is also an important driver of the synergistic effect of mixed litter decomposition via N transfer among different litter types (Lummer et al., 2012; Handa et al., 2014; Schimel and Hättenschwiler, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Under N limiting conditions, microbes in decomposing litters can acquire N via multiple pathways, including retention of N released from higher quality litters, reuse of N from microbial necromass, and immobilization of N from the soil pool.
source: Under N limiting conditions, microbes in decomposing litters can acquire N via multiple pathways, including retention of N released from higher quality litters, reuse of N from microbial necromass, and immobilization of N from the soil pool (Schimel and Hättenschwiler, 2007; Vos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: All litter mixtures as well as single litter species included in the meta-analysis showed net N release.
source: Overall, however, all litter mixtures as well as single litter species included in our meta-analysis showed net N release (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no relationship between the number of species included in mixtures and the effect size.
source: Our global analysis clearly shows that there was no relationship between the number of species included in mixtures and the effect size (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Mixture effects did not increase with species richness.
source: In other words, mixture effects did not increase with species richness.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Species composition was far more important than how many species contributed to the mixture.
source: This was also shown in a number of previous case studies (Barantal et al., 2014; Lin and Zeng, 2018; Wardle et al., 1997), which argued that the species composition was far more important than how many species contributed to the mixture.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Leaves from evergreen species commonly have longer lifespans, higher lignin concentrations, and higher ratios of lignin:N and C:N than leaves from deciduous species.
source: Leaves from evergreen species commonly have longer lifespans, higher lignin concentrations, and higher ratios of lignin:N and C:N (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and thus a priori slower decomposition rates than leaves from deciduous species (Aerts, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the text, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and cited from previous research.

claim: Evergreen species have slower decomposition rates than deciduous species.
source: Leaves from evergreen species commonly have longer lifespans, higher lignin concentrations, and higher ratios of lignin:N and C:N (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and thus a priori slower decomposition rates than leaves from deciduous species (Aerts, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Mixing deciduous species resulted in similarly strong synergistic effects compared to mixing deciduous with evergreen species.
source: However, our results only partly confirm this expectation, because mixing deciduous species resulted in similarly strong synergistic effects compared to mixing deciduous with evergreen species (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Interactions between rapidly decomposing and N-fixing species, both deciduous, were driving mixture effects, rather than interactions between deciduous and evergreen.
source: Indeed, in a previous large-scale study covering forests from five different biomes, Handa et al., 2014 showed that interactions between rapidly decomposing and N-fixing species, both deciduous, were driving mixture effects, rather than interactions between deciduous and evergreen.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Ca and Mg can increase decomposition by stimulating the growth and activity of white rot fungi.
source: It has been suggested that Ca and Mg can increase decomposition by stimulating the growth and activity of white rot fungi (Eriksson et al., 1990), which may then contribute to N transfer among litter types (García‐Palacios et al., 2016), potentially explaining the overall strong mixing effects when at least one litter species of high micronutrient concentrations was present in the mixture (thus resulting in high divergence).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: About two thirds of the Ca, Mg and K concentration data are from the tropical biome.
source: It should be noted that initial litter quality variables have not been evenly measured across all biomes. For example, about two thirds of the Ca, Mg and K concentration data are from the tropical biome, which may dominate the cation divergence effects on mixed litter decomposition.
evidence: This is a statement about the dataset composition.

claim: The pattern of increasing mixture effects with increasing divergence in Ca and Mg remained robust even when data from Butenschoen et al., 2014 were excluded from the analysis.
source: The pattern of increasing mixture effects with increasing divergence in Ca and Mg, however, remained robust even when these data were excluded from the analysis (see Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Litter quality parameters other than N, C:N or lignin:N ratios are particularly poorly documented for forests in the boreal, Mediterranean and subtropical biomes.
source: Litter quality parameters other than N, C:N or lignin:N ratios are particularly poorly documented for forests in the boreal, Mediterranean and subtropical biomes, which makes it presently difficult to compare biome-specific relationships or to draw robust conclusions about the generality of the reported relationships between divergence in litter quality and mixture effects on mass loss.
evidence: This is an observation about the available literature.

claim: Under natural conditions, different plant species do not typically contribute equally to the leaf litter pool on forest floors.
source: Under natural conditions, different plant species do not typically contribute equally to the leaf litter pool on forest floors (King, 2002; Schuster and Dukes, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: According to the mass ratio hypothesis, the dominance of certain litter species is expected to prime litter mixture effects.
source: According to the mass ratio hypothesis (Grime, 1998), the dominance of certain litter species is expected to prime litter mixture effects, which therefore could differ depending on how evenly the different litter species are represented in a mixture.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Mixtures showed consistently positive effects on mass loss regardless of the relative abundance of litters in a mixture.
source: Our comparison between even and uneven litter mixtures does not suggest fundamental differences with shifts in evenness, as mixtures showed consistently positive effects on mass loss regardless of the relative abundance of litters in a mixture (Figure 4), although mixtures with uneven contributions of the different litter species tended to produce slightly stronger synergistic effects.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Changes in species evenness of litter mixtures had no effect on decomposition.
source: However, overall our results are consistent with a previous study showing that changes in species evenness of litter mixtures had no effect on decomposition (King, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Mixture effects are not necessarily regulated by the dominant species as would be predicted by the mass ratio hypothesis.
source: Collectively this indicates that mixture effects are not necessarily regulated by the dominant species (Dj et al., 2013) as would be predicted by the mass ratio hypothesis.
evidence: This is an inference from the data supported by citation.

claim: Mass ratio and resource complementarity both act at the same time to a variable degree, depending on environmental conditions.
source: A recent study that explicitly tested for the relative importance of mass ratio and resource complementarity in mixed litter decomposition reported that they both act at the same time to a variable degree, depending on environmental conditions (García-Palacios et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Natural forests normally possess greater species diversity than planted forests.
source: Although natural forests normally possess greater species diversity than planted forests (Halpern and Spies, 1995), synergistic interactions emerged in both types of forests, with somewhat stronger effects in plantations on average (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Synergistic interactions emerged in both natural and planted forests, with somewhat stronger effects in plantations on average.
source: Although natural forests normally possess greater species diversity than planted forests (Halpern and Spies, 1995), synergistic interactions emerged in both types of forests, with somewhat stronger effects in plantations on average (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The weaker effects in litter mixtures from canopy trees in planted forests may reflect the artificial canopy composition through the selection of economically valuable tree species.
source: Nonetheless, the weaker effects in litter mixtures from canopy trees in planted forests may reflect the artificial canopy composition through the selection of economically valuable tree species.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data patterns.

claim: The understory community in plantations may still be relatively close to that from a more natural forest, which may explain their contribution to synergistic litter mixture effects in plantations.
source: On the other hand, the understory community may still be relatively close to that from a more natural forest, which may explain their contribution to synergistic litter mixture effects in plantations.

claim: For forest management, the understory vegetation has a particularly important role for biogeochemical cycling when forests are managed as plantations.

claim: Partial exclusion of the decomposer food web can lead to changes in decomposition.
source: Partial exclusion of the decomposer food web can lead to changes in decomposition (Bokhorst and Wardle, 2013; Bradford et al., 2002) and the complexity and diversity of decomposer organisms can be an important driver of litter mixture effects (Barantal et al., 2014; Handa et al., 2014; Hättenschwiler and Gasser, 2005; Vos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The complexity and diversity of decomposer organisms can be an important driver of litter mixture effects.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Soil fauna are important in mediating mixture decomposition.
source: This is a surprising result, because soil fauna are important in mediating mixture decomposition as found in several litterbag studies using different mesh sizes and reporting stronger non-additive effects with larger mesh size (Barantal et al., 2014; Martins et al., 2010; Schädler and Brandl, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Almost three quarters of all temperate forest studies used the intermediate mesh size.
source: For example, almost three quarters of all temperate forest studies used the intermediate mesh size.

claim: 51% of all observations for larger mesh size are from tropical forests.
source: On the other hand, 51% of all observations for larger mesh size are from tropical forests where leaf litter may contain high amounts of polyphenols that may prevent macrofauna feeding (Hättenschwiler and Vitousek, 2000).
evidence: This is a statement about the dataset composition.

claim: Leaf litter in tropical forests may contain high amounts of polyphenols that may prevent macrofauna feeding.

source: Indeed, we found slightly antagonistic effects for the largest mesh size in tropical forests but not in the other biomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Mixed litter decomposes more rapidly and releases N at higher rates than single-species litter.
source: Taken together, our quantitative synthesis of litter mixture effects on decomposition in forest ecosystems suggests that mixed litter decomposes more rapidly and releases N at higher rates than single-species litter.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the meta-analysis.

claim: These responses are robust for temperate forests, but need confirmation for boreal, Mediterranean, subtropical, and tropical forests that are presently data-limited.
source: These responses are robust for temperate forests, but need confirmation for boreal, Mediterranean, subtropical, and tropical forests that are presently data-limited.

claim: Trait divergence in litter mixtures was identified as a major driver of litter mixture effects in early decomposition stages.
source: Future studies should focus on these presently understudied forest ecosystems by addressing trait divergence in litter mixtures more specifically, which we identified as a major driver of litter mixture effects in early decomposition stages.

claim: Biodiversity loss will modify C and nutrient cycling in forest ecosystems, with the magnitude and direction of changes depending on the complexity of the decomposer communities, litter species properties, and biome.
source: Based on our results, we conclude that biodiversity loss will modify C and nutrient cycling in forest ecosystems, with the magnitude and direction of changes depending on the complexity of the decomposer communities, litter species properties, and biome.
